Type.evidence_source: [/page/7/Text/10] It varied how long it took the participants to disclose their trauma, but they all had in common that it was initially hard for them.

Area.evidence_source: [/page/7/Text/10] Their conclusion is that disclosure is a difficult and complex process and male stereotypes have created such an environment for men that disclosure is hard for them. Alaggia and Mishna (32) found in their study that male survivors find it hard to disclose violence, among other things, because they find it difficult to regard themselves as victims, especially in the case of sexual violence. We found this in the cases where women were the perpetrators. Men's difficulties regarding disclosure can also be linked to the social belief that sexual violence rarely happens to boys and it complicates matters further, and even becomes a taboo to talk about, when victims and perpetrators are of the same sex (33). Furthermore, men who report violence often face disbelief and diminishment and are, therefore, very reluctant to disclose, and thus, the risk of the violence lasting longer increases, the perpetrators will keep on violating boys and men, and some victims will probably never disclose (33). [...] In our study, the men experienced an intense relief when they did disclose their trauma. Trauma-specific support was important for them and the most valuable support came from fellow male survivors.
